```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5,
                      warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

Most diet questions are comparisons: before and after a change in the
ecosystem, small and large predators, one region and another. In DietView a
comparison starts with a covariate, a column you declare in `dv_spec()`. This
article shows how to build covariates from years and lengths, how to count
what each level holds before reading it, how to draw one sunburst per level so
the panels can be compared, and how to cross two covariates.

It uses the public ICES stomach data that ship with the package (ICES Stomach
Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed with the R package
stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see `?ices_diet`), restricted to the four predators
with the most prey records. The data were not collected to answer any of the
comparisons below: the strata are uneven, and part of the article is about
seeing that before drawing conclusions.

```{r setup}
library(DietView)

# drop non-food items and nematodes (mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]

four <- c("Atlantic cod", "Atlantic mackerel", "European plaice", "Whiting")
dat  <- dat[dat$predator_common %in% four, ]
table(dat$predator_common)
```

## 1. Build covariates from years and lengths

`region`, `year` and `quarter` are already columns of the data. Two more are
built here: a period from the year and a length class from the predator's
length.

### Periods

`dv_add_period()` cuts years into periods. Look at the years first:

```{r years}
table(dat$predator_common, dat$year)
```

Only cod spans several years. Mackerel were sampled in 2022 only and plaice
in 2024 only, so a period comparison is a cod (and partly whiting) question.
We compare 2022 with 2023-2024. The obvious call,
`dv_add_period(year, breaks = c(2021, 2022, 2024))`, would put 2021 into the
first period with 2022, because the first period includes its lower break.
Make the choice explicit instead:

```{r period}
dat$period <- dv_add_period(dat$year, breaks = c(2021.5, 2022, 2024),
                            labels = c("2022", "2023-2024"))
table(dat$year, dat$period, useNA = "ifany")
```

The `r sum(dat$year < 2022)` records from 2020 and 2021 now have no period
(`NA`). They stay in the data and in every other comparison; they are only
left out of the period panels. A year equal to an inner break belongs to the
earlier period, so 2022 falls in the first one.

### Length classes

`dv_size_bins()` cuts lengths into bins. Predators differ in size, so give
each its own breaks:

```{r size-ranges}
sapply(split(dat$length_cm, dat$predator_common), range)
```

```{r size-bins}
breaks <- list(
  "Atlantic cod"      = c(0, 20, 35, 50, 110),
  "Whiting"           = c(0, 20, 30, 50),
  "Atlantic mackerel" = c(15, 30, 35, 50),
  "European plaice"   = c(10, 20, 30, 60)
)
dat$size_bin <- NA_character_
for (p in names(breaks)) {
  i <- dat$predator_common == p
  dat$size_bin[i] <- as.character(dv_size_bins(dat$length_cm[i], breaks[[p]]))
}
table(dat$predator_common, dat$size_bin, useNA = "ifany")
```

The breaks are a choice you make on biology and state in your methods. Here
the cod and whiting breaks bracket the lengths at which these gadoids turn
from crustaceans to fish; the mackerel and plaice breaks split the juveniles
from the larger adults. Each bin includes its lower edge (`right = FALSE`), so
a 20 cm cod is in `[20, 35)`. Every break vector covers the whole range shown
above; a length outside the breaks would get no bin. Check the table for `NA`
before you go on.

### Declare them

```{r prep}
spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",
  prey_name      = "prey_name",
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter", "period", "size_bin")
)
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)
```

## 2. Count what each level holds

A level is worth reading only if it holds enough stomachs. Count stomachs, not
records: records within a stomach are not independent.

```{r counts}
n_stom <- function(d, v) {
  tapply(d$stomach_id, list(d$predator_common, d[[v]]),
         function(z) length(unique(z)))
}
d <- prep$data
n_stom(d, "region")
n_stom(d, "quarter")
n_stom(d, "period")
```

`dv_summary(prep, by = "region")` gives the same counts with the number of
records and prey taxa. The empty cells (`NA`) are combinations that were never
sampled: no mackerel from the Baltic, no plaice in quarters 2 or 4. A
comparison across a covariate is possible only for the predators that occur in
more than one of its levels.

## 3. One palette for every panel

Build the colors once, from the tree of all records, so that a taxon has the
same color in every panel. With several hundred prey taxa, `dv_palette()`
would have to reuse its 20 colors many times; `dv_palette_tree()` gives one
hue per phylum and lighter tints to the taxa below it:

```{r palette}
tree_all <- dv_tree(prep)
pal <- dv_palette_tree(tree_all)
length(pal)
```

The palette is keyed by node, so it works for any tree built from a subset of
these records.

## 4. Cod in 2022 and in 2023-2024

```{r cod}
cod <- d[d$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ]

t22 <- dv_build_tree(cod[cod$period %in% "2022", ], prep$ranks,
                     weight_col = spec$weight)
t34 <- dv_build_tree(cod[cod$period %in% "2023-2024", ], prep$ranks,
                     weight_col = spec$weight)
```

```{r sunburst-p1}
dv_sunburst(t22, mode = "weight", colors = pal, title = "Atlantic cod, 2022",
            subtitle = "share of prey weight")
```

```{r sunburst-p2}
dv_sunburst(t34, mode = "weight", colors = pal, title = "Atlantic cod, 2023-2024",
            subtitle = "share of prey weight")
```

How to read two panels side by side: both start at the same angle and list
taxa in the same order, so you read them in the same direction. A taxon does
not always sit at the same angle, though. If it is absent from one period,
every wedge after it moves round to close the gap. Use color, not position,
to find a taxon in both panels, and the hover labels to read its share.

To compare numbers rather than pictures, put the two rank tables side by side.
Each column is a share of that period's records (or weight), unidentified
records included, so each column adds up to 100:

```{r compare}
side_by_side <- function(ta, tb, names, rank = "Class") {
  a <- dv_rank_table(ta, rank)
  b <- dv_rank_table(tb, rank)
  a <- a[a$label != "NA", c("label", "pct_occ", "pct_w")]
  b <- b[b$label != "NA", c("label", "pct_occ", "pct_w")]
  m <- merge(a, b, by = "label", all = TRUE, suffixes = paste0("_", names))
  m[is.na(m)] <- 0
  m[, -1] <- round(m[, -1], 1)
  m[order(-m[[2]]), ][1:5, ]
}
side_by_side(t22, t34, c("2022", "2023_24"))
```

```{r compare-num, include = FALSE}
cmp <- side_by_side(t22, t34, c("2022", "2023_24"))
mal <- cmp[cmp$label == "Malacostraca", ]
tel <- cmp[cmp$label == "Teleostei", ]
```

By weight, crustaceans fall from `r mal$pct_w_2022`% of the cod diet in 2022
to `r mal$pct_w_2023_24`% in 2023-2024, and fish rise from
`r tel$pct_w_2022`% to `r tel$pct_w_2023_24`%. Before calling this a change in
time, look at what else differs between the two periods:

```{r confounding}
n_stom(cod, "period")
tapply(cod$stomach_id, list(cod$region, cod$period), function(z) length(unique(z)))
tapply(cod$stomach_id, list(cod$size_bin, cod$period), function(z) length(unique(z)))
```

All the 2022 cod come from the North Sea, while 2023-2024 adds the Baltic and
the Skagerrak-Kattegat; and the 2022 sample has proportionally more small cod.
The two periods differ in region and in predator size as much as in time, so
the difference in the panels cannot be attributed to the period alone. This is
the usual situation with survey data assembled after the fact: read the
sampling design off the counts before you read the diet off the panels.

## 5. Cod by length class and by region

Length gives a cleaner contrast, because it varies within every region and
period. A small helper puts the stomach count next to the share of fish
(Teleostei) in each level:

```{r size}
fish_by <- function(x, v) {
  trees <- lapply(split(x, x[[v]]), function(s)
    dv_build_tree(s, prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight))
  out <- t(sapply(trees, function(t) {
    r <- dv_rank_table(t, "Class")
    c(fish_records_pct = round(sum(r$pct_occ[r$label == "Teleostei"]), 1),
      fish_weight_pct  = round(sum(r$pct_w[r$label == "Teleostei"]), 1))
  }))
  cbind(stomachs = n_stom(x, v)[1, rownames(out)], out)
}
by_size <- lapply(split(cod, cod$size_bin), function(x)
  dv_build_tree(x, prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight))

fish_share <- fish_by(cod, "size_bin")
fish_share
```

```{r size-num, include = FALSE}
fs <- fish_share
```

The share of fish in the cod diet rises steadily with cod length, from
`r fs[1, "fish_weight_pct"]`% of the prey weight below 20 cm to
`r fs[nrow(fs), "fish_weight_pct"]`% above 50 cm. The two ends of the size
range, with the same palette:

```{r sunburst-small}
dv_sunburst(by_size[["[0, 20)"]], mode = "weight", colors = pal,
            title = "Atlantic cod, under 20 cm", subtitle = "share of prey weight")
```

```{r sunburst-large}
dv_sunburst(by_size[["[50, 110)"]], mode = "weight", colors = pal,
            title = "Atlantic cod, 50 cm and over", subtitle = "share of prey weight")
```

The same lines work for any of the four predators; only the breaks differ.

By region:

```{r region}
fish_by(cod, "region")
```

```{r region-num, include = FALSE}
fr <- fish_by(cod, "region")
```

At class level the regions are close. Fish make up `r fr["Baltic Sea", "fish_weight_pct"]`% of the cod prey weight
in the Baltic Sea, `r fr["North Sea", "fish_weight_pct"]`% in the North Sea
and `r fr["Skagerrak-Kattegat", "fish_weight_pct"]`% in the
Skagerrak-Kattegat, where only `r fr["Skagerrak-Kattegat", "stomachs"]`
stomachs were sampled, all in one year. Region, like period, is entangled with
the other covariates: the Baltic and Skagerrak-Kattegat cod were all caught in
2023-2024, and their length distributions differ from the North Sea one. A
table of stomachs by region and length class (`n_stom()` on a crossed
variable, or the crossed panels below) is the first thing to look at before
interpreting any of these differences.

## 6. Crossing two covariates

Often the question is one covariate within another: does the diet of large cod
differ between periods in the same way as that of small ones? First count what
each combination holds:

```{r cross}
cells <- tapply(cod$stomach_id, list(cod$size_bin, cod$period),
                function(z) length(unique(z)))
cells
```

Crossing divides the sample quickly. With
`r sum(!is.na(cod$period))` cod records split into eight cells, the largest
cod of 2022 come from only `r cells["[50, 110)", "2022"]` stomachs. Decide in
advance how many stomachs a cell needs before you interpret it, and report
that number with the figure. With a minimum of 30 stomachs, for example, the
cells to read are:

```{r cross-keep}
which(cells >= 30, arr.ind = TRUE)
```

Draw a cell only when it passes:

```{r cross-one}
sub <- cod[cod$size_bin == "[20, 35)" & cod$period %in% "2023-2024", ]
tc  <- dv_build_tree(sub, prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight)
dv_sunburst(tc, mode = "occurrence", colors = pal,
            title = "Atlantic cod, 20-35 cm, 2023-2024",
            subtitle = paste(length(unique(sub$stomach_id)), "stomachs; share of prey records"))
```

The Shiny app does the same interactively: choose a covariate under **Facet by
covariate** and a second one under **Cross with**, and it draws one panel per
combination (`run_dietview(prep)`).

## 7. A missing level is not an unidentified prey

Two kinds of `NA` appear in this article, and they mean different things.

A covariate `NA` is a record that belongs to no level of the covariate: here
the `r sum(is.na(d$period))` records from 2020 and 2021, which have no period.
They are not in any period panel. The dashboard leaves such records out of that
covariate's row of panels, and the Shiny app shows them in a separate "NA"
panel, so you can see what was set aside.

A taxonomic `NA` is a prey record not identified to a rank: a white wedge
inside every panel, kept so that each ring still adds up to 100%. It has
nothing to do with the covariates:

```{r two-nas}
c(period_na_records    = sum(is.na(d$period)),
  class_na_records_cod = sum(is.na(cod$class)))
```

Report the first as a sample size ("`r sum(is.na(cod$period))` cod records
from 2021 were not assigned a period") and the second as an identification
share ("`r round(100 * mean(is.na(cod$class)), 1)`% of the cod prey records
were not identified to class").

## 8. All strata in one file

`dv_build_html()` writes every comparison into one HTML file: `strata` gives
each covariate its own row of sunbursts, and `cross` adds crossed rows.
`cross = list(c(inner, outer))` reads "inner within outer": one row per level
of `outer`, one sunburst per level of `inner` in that row.

```{r dash, eval = FALSE}
dv_build_html(prep, output = file.path(tempdir(), "ices_by_strata.html"),
              strata = c("region", "quarter", "period", "size_bin"),
              cross  = list(c("size_bin", "period"),    # length classes within periods
                            c("size_bin", "region")),   # length classes within regions
              length_col = "length_cm")
```

The dashboard draws every cell that holds records, whatever its size, and shows the number of
stomachs in each. The small-cell rule is yours to apply when you read it. By
default the build stays offline; see the species-cards article for predator
photos from iNaturalist, with their authors and licenses.
